sentences.text: Claosaurus means broken lizard because the fossils were discovered in an unusual position.
The only valid species known today is Claosaurus agilis.
Scientists cannot determine the exact size of the adult animal because the fossil record is incomplete.
This bipedal herbivore had a slender body, long hind legs, and small forelimbs.
Estimates suggest the creature measured about 3.5 meters in length and weighed about 475 kilograms.
Thomas Holtz estimated the mass of the animal to be similar to that of a lion.
Fossils were first found in 1871 in the Niobrara Formation near the Smoky Hill River in Kansas.
The animal was originally named Hadrosaurus agilis in 1872 but was renamed Claosaurus agilis in 1890.
Joseph Gregory corrected the holotype status in 1948 by identifying three toe bones from the right foot.
Claosaurus was an herbivore, like other hadrosaurs.
Reports of gastroliths in Claosaurus are based on a probable double misidentification of the specimen.
The specimen thought to have gastroliths was originally misidentified as Claosaurus by Barnum Brown in 1900.
It is believed that Claosaurus moved on two legs but supported itself on all four limbs while feeding.
While traditionally classified as an early hadrosaurid, a 2008 analysis placed Claosaurus outside the Hadrosauridae clade.
A 2008 analysis found Claosaurus agilis outside the clade containing Hadrosaurus and other hadrosaurids.
Claosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous Period in what is now North America.
Claosaurus agilis lived approximately 80 million years ago during the Campanian stage.
The time range for Claosaurus is from the Coniacian to the Campanian, between 89.8 and 72.2 million years ago.
A second species, C. annectens, was named in 1892 but was later reassigned to the genus Edmontosaurus.
G. R. Wieland named a third species, C. affinis, in 1903 based on remains from the Pierre Shale of South Dakota.
The remains used to describe C. affinis were found in the Pierre Shale of South Dakota in association with the giant sea turtle Archelon.
A 2004 review by Jack Horner and colleagues considered C. affinis a dubious hadrosaur, reporting its type material as lost.
